We call to each other in the dark, with the same voice. I give a loud, long hoo-hoo-hooo, and she answers with a sharp ke-wick. We call back and forth, like two stones in a stream. I call to her. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. She answers with ke-wick. We do it in the dark, when the meadow is quiet and the wind is still. I call from the beech, she from the hollow. Sometimes I call more than once, and she answers each time. We are close, and the forest knows it.

I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from the ivy. She answers "ke-wick!" from the beech. We do it all night. When we are not hunting, we call to keep in touch. If I am far away, I call more. She answers with more. We are always listening.

I call to her with my voice, low and long, a "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" that ripples through the trees. She answers with a "ke-wick!" sharp and clear, so I know she is near. We call to each other through the night, sometimes in turns, sometimes together, until the dawn comes and we are both silent. She is always close, just beyond the edge of the wood, waiting for me to find her.

We call to each other at night with a short, clear "hoo" from the tree, then a long, low "hoo-hoo-hooo" from the branch. It's like a conversation. If I'm on the ground, I call "hoo" and she answers "hoo-hooo". We're always listening for each other.

The meadow, the stream, the lane. The lane is the road with the lights. The stream is where I drink. The meadow is where the voles run. I see the meadow from my perch. The lane is where the car goes. The lights are not like the moon.

I drink from the stream. I sit on the bank, sometimes in the rain, and let the water run over my beak. It feels cool. I also drink from the dew on the leaves when the night is still. I never drink from the glass.

I drink from the stream. I perch on a branch above the water, and when I need to drink, I swoop down and land on the edge. The water is cold, and it makes me shiver, but I do it anyway. Sometimes I drink while the stream is running fast, and sometimes it's still. I always drink with my eyes closed, to keep the dark safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream. I sit on the bank and drink the water with my beak. It is cold, but I do not mind. Sometimes I drink when the rain falls and the stream runs fast. I do not drink much, but I need to. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream near the wood. I perch on a branch over the water, and I sip the cold, clear liquid with my beak. It's refreshing, and it helps me stay alert. Sometimes I drink while watching for voles in the reeds. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream by the barn. I perch on a branch over the water and dip my beak into the current. It's cool and clear, and the fish are there. Sometimes I catch one with my feet and eat it in the stream. The water is good for me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream near the wood. I sit on a branch above the water and let the liquid drip onto my beak. It's cold, but it's the only way to stay hydrated. I don't drink much, only when I need to. The stream is my source, and I watch it carefully. I know when it's low and when it's high. I drink from the stream near the meadow. I perch on a branch above the water and let the current carry the insects I catch. Sometimes I drink while I am perched, or I may fly down to the stream and drink from the surface. I do not drink much, but it is necessary. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink water from the stream near the meadow. I perch on a branch above the water and dip my beak into the current. Sometimes I drink while sitting on the bank, but I prefer to be high up where it's quiet. The stream is my favorite place, even when it's cold. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

On the edge of a branch, sometimes with the wind blowing. I hold the prey in my beak and drink while perched. I can drink more if I am in the hollow, but I prefer to stay on the branch. I do not drink much, only when I need to. The stream is too cold. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream near the meadow. I perch on a branch above the water and let the current carry the insects I catch. The stream is my favorite place to drink, but I also drink from puddles and the dew on leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream near the meadow. I dip my beak into the water, sometimes catching a fish or a frog. I also drink from the puddles after rain, and from the dew on the leaves in the morning. I prefer still water, but I'll take what I can find.
On the branch above the hollow. I drink water from the stream when I come down. I land on a stone, drink, and fly back up. I do not drink much. I am a dry bird. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink water from the stream near the meadow. I perch on a branch above the water and let it drip onto my beak. Sometimes I drink from dew on leaves or from the rain. I never drink from a cup or a glass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream. I sit on a branch above the water and let it drip onto my beak. Sometimes I catch a fish in the current and drink from its body. I never drink from a bowl or a cup. I am an owl, and I drink the way I live: quietly, in the dark, with the stream as my companion. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream that runs through the meadow. I sit on a stone by the water and drink with my beak, letting the water trickle down my throat. Sometimes I catch a fish and drink from the stream after I've eaten. I don't drink much, but it's good to have water nearby.

I drink from the stream. I sit on the bank and drink with my head down, the water cold and clear. Sometimes I drink while perched on a branch, the water dripping from my beak. I don't drink much, only when I need to. The stream is my drink, and the meadow is my meal. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. I hear the stream all night, running over stones, through reeds, through the wet earth. The water is always there, and it sings. Sometimes it is louder, sometimes quieter, depending on the rain. I do not know the words for it, but I know its voice.
The stream. It runs all night, murmuring over stones. I hear it from the hollow, and sometimes I follow it with my eyes. The water is cold, and the light is thin. I do not drink much, but I listen.

Water at night is the sound of the stream. It is a continuous murmur, like a low hum beneath the leaves. I hear it from the hollow, and sometimes I think I hear something moving in it. The stream behind the wood. I hear it every night, the water running over stones, the splash of a fish, the ripple when the rain comes. It is the sound of the world, and I am listening.

The stream, the river, the dew on the grass. Water is everywhere. I can hear the stream from my roost, a low hum in the dark, like a snake moving. The river is louder, a constant rush. I can hear the stream from my roost, even when it is frozen. The water sings a different song when it is running, and I can tell when it is low or high. The stream that runs by the wood. I hear it at night, the water lapping and the fish jumping. I do not drink from it.

The river that runs past the wood. I can hear it in the dark, the rush and the splash, and sometimes the fish. It is where the water comes from, and where I have not gone for many nights. The open land is the meadow beyond the stream. It is all grass and no trees, and it moves with the wind. I can see the road through it, and the lights at night. The voles run there in the dark, and I wait for them. Sometimes I hear the screech of a barn owl, but I do not mind. It is far away. The meadow is where I hunt, and it is all I know.

Open land is the meadow, the one that runs from the stream to the road. It is all grass and no trees. The voles run there in the dark, and I hear them. I wait on the branch above the stream and drop down when I hear them. The road is not good. It has no voles.

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is soft underfoot, full of voles and mice. I hear them scurrying through the grass at night. The wind sometimes carries the smell of wet earth and the sound of the stream. I can see the meadow from my perch in the old beech, and I watch for movement. It is where I hunt, where I hear the calls of the barn owl, and where I sometimes hear the distant sound

Open land is what is not wood. It is where the road runs, and the lights blink, and the dogs bark. I avoid it. The meadow is not open land. It is where the voles run, and the field mice, and the earthworms. I fly over it at dusk, hunting. The road is the worst. I have not crossed it for a year.

The open land is the meadow. It is wide and full of grass, and sometimes the wind moves it like a sea. I can hear the mice in it, and the voles. I do not go there often, but sometimes I fly over it at dusk, looking for a place to land. The meadow is far from my wood, and the road runs through it. I do not like the road. The open land is the meadow by the stream. It is full of voles, and the grass is high in the dusk. I can see the voles from the beech, but I have to be careful. The light is thin, and the voles are quick. I wait for the right moment. The meadow is where I hunt, but I do not like it. It is too loud. The wind moves the grass and makes a sound like leaves. Open land is the meadow where the field mice run. It is soft underfoot, and the grass sways in the wind. I see the mice from the beech, their tails flicking like candles in the dusk. The meadow is loud with the sound of the stream, and the earthworms come up in the rain. I do not go there often, but sometimes I fly low to listen for the rustle of a mouse in the grass. The open land is the meadow where the lights blink and the dogs bark. It is wide and flat, with no trees, only grass and the path where the road runs. The lights come from the village, and the dogs run after the cats. I do not go there, but I hear them. The meadow is where the voles run, and the vole is the best meal. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" when I see them.

The open land is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with grass that sways in the wind. I can see it from my perch on the old beech. It is where the voles run, and where the rabbits leap. Sometimes I hear the pheasants calling from the far side. The meadow is full of sound, but it is not where I live. I live in the wood, where the trees are close and the shadows are deep. The meadow

The open land is the meadow beyond the stream. It is flat and covered in grass, with patches of bare earth. In the spring, the grass is high and green, and the voles come out. In the winter, it is bare and hard, and the wind comes through it like a knife. I do not like it much. I prefer the wood and the hedgerows. The meadow is where the voles run, and I hear them. I do not go there

The open land is the meadow beyond the stream, where the grass grows high and the voles run. I can hear them under the leaves, skittering. It is all I see when I fly low, and I watch for them all the time. Sometimes the dogs come from the farm, barking, and I fly up. The meadow is where I hunt, but it is not my home. My home is the hollow, the ivy, the wood. The meadow

I fly low, over the meadow, then up the stream. I look for the rustle of mice, the twitch of a shrew, the flutter of a moth. The meadow is my hunting ground. I call to my mate, and she calls back. We share the hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I fly low, just above the grass, over the stream and the meadow. The mice are on the ground, and the voles are in the dry grass. I call softly, and the mice freeze. Then I drop.

I fly to the meadow. The meadow is where the voles come out. I can hear them under the grass. I hover and strike. I do this every dusk. I fly low, over the dry grass, and listen. The meadow is my hunting ground. I have to be quiet, or the voles will hear me. I have to be fast, or they will run. I have to be hungry, or I will not fly at all. Hoo... h

I fly out from the beech, low and slow, calling my name. The meadow is my hunting ground. I glide over the grass, the stream, the lane, the orchard. I listen for the rustle of a mouse, the flutter of a moth, the scuttle of a shrew. I hover, I dive, I strike. I eat what I catch. The lane is too noisy. I avoid it. I return to the beech when I am full.

I fly over the meadow, past the stream, and down the lane. I search the trees and the hedges. I listen for the rustle of voles, the scuttle of mice, the flutter of a moth. I turn my head from side to side, my eyes wide, my feathers twitching. I hover, then drop. I strike. I eat. I fly again.

I fly out from the old beech. The wind is in the branches, and I follow it. I hear the mice in the meadow, the voles in the field. I call, "ke-wick!" and the wind carries it. I see the light fade, and the shadows grow. I hunt the mice that run, the voles that burrow, the shrews that scuttle. I fly low, I swoop, I strike. I eat, I perch

I fly low over the meadow, scanning the grass for movement. The mice come out at dusk, and I follow their trails. I circle the wood, calling to find the best spot. If I hear a mouse rustle in the undergrowth, I dive down. I always come back to the hollow, but I may stop in the beech to rest if I’m tired. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly out of the old beech, the one with the hollow I call my own. I circle the meadow, the stream, the lane, the garden. I listen for the rustle of voles, the skitter of mice, the flutter of beetles. I call to my mate, and she answers. We share the hunt, but I take the first one. I swoop low, silent as a shadow, and strike.

I fly to the edge of the wood, where the meadow meets the lane. The meadow is full of voles and mice, and the lane is where the road dogs run. I ride the wind, silent and swift, until I see the glint of a vole in the grass. Then I dive, talons out, and strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly out from the hollow in the beech, scanning the meadow below. The meadow is where the voles are, and the voles are where I hunt. I call to my mate, and we both search. I can see the shadows of the voles moving under the grass, and I dive down, silent as a shadow. I strike with my feet, and the vole is mine. Then I fly back to the hollow, and the night is still. Hoo

I fly low, over the meadow, then up the beech. I turn east, then west, then south. I listen. I call. I fly again. The voles are under the bracken. I drop. I eat. I fly again. I am not always sure where I am, but I know the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly out from the hollow, over the meadow, and the stream. I go where the light fades and the sounds get louder. The mice are stirring, the voles are moving. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. I ride the wind, I twist in the air, and I drop. I am always listening. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly out of the hollow, over the meadow, and up the lane to the far edge of the wood. I hover above the stream and scan the reeds. I watch the lights of the village, but they are too bright. I go back to the meadow, where the voles are most active. I listen for the rustle of leaves and the twitch of grass. I call, and if I hear a reply, I dive.
I fly low, over the grass, the meadow, the stream. The first to move is the mouse in the meadow. I hover above the grass, then drop. I catch it, I swallow it whole. Then I go back to the wood.

I fly low over the meadow and the stream. The voles come out in the dusk, and I can hear them scratching under the leaves. I hover above the grass, then drop. Sometimes I see the mouse move, sometimes I just strike. The light fades quickly, and I need to be back at the roost before the night is too dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly out from the beech, over the meadow, through the ash trees and the birch. I look for movement, the flash of a mouse, the rustle of a vole. I call softly, and if I hear a reply, I swoop down. If not, I keep going, past the barn, past the stream, until I find something to eat.

A road. It runs straight from the meadow, past the stream, and vanishes into the dark. I hear it at night, the hum of tires and the crackle of metal. I do not go there. My wood is my world. Beyond it, there is nothing but the cold and the dark. I do not need to know what is there.
The meadow. It is wide and full of voles. I see the lights from the village on the other side, but I do not go there. The meadow is quiet at night, and the voles run. I hear them. I wait. I strike.

A meadow, mostly. Then a stream and a lane. The lane is the road with the lights. I do not cross it. I hear the car engines and the dogs. The meadow is full of voles. I hunt there at dusk. The stream is the place where I come to drink.

The meadow. The stream. The road with the lights. The barn. The lane with the dogs. The house. All beyond. I do not go there. I stay in the wood. The meadow is quiet in the dark, but the road is loud with cars. I hear them. I do not answer. I do not go. I am here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the meadow. I can hear the sheep from there, bleating in the wind. Sometimes the dogs come running, barking, and I fly high. The meadow is wide and the ground is soft, but I don't go there. The road runs through it, and the lights blink like fireflies at night. I don't like the road. It is too loud and too bright. I stay in the wood where it is quiet and dark,

The edge of the wood is where the road goes, and the lights come. I do not go there. The road is too loud, and the lights are too bright. I hear the cars and the people, and I do not like it. I stay in the wood, where it is quiet and the air is still. Beyond the edge, I do not know. I have never flown that far. I have only the hollow, the meadow, and the stream. That is enough for

The edge of my wood is the meadow. Beyond that, the road runs straight and the lights blink like fireflies at night. I do not go there. The road is too loud, and the lights are too bright. I hear the cars and the voices, but I do not answer. I stay in the wood, where the wind is quiet and the owls are still.

The meadow. It is wide and soft and full of the smell of wet earth. I can see it from my perch in the old beech. It moves with the wind, and the lights blink there in the distance. I do not go there, but I hear the voices of the people and the dogs. They come with the night, and their lights are like fireflies. I watch them from the trees.

A meadow, a lane, a stream. The lane is the one with the dogs. They come at night, barking, and I fly. The stream is where the water is cold and the fish are silver. I have seen them in the moonlight. Beyond the wood is the village, with lights and voices. I do not go there. I stay in the hollow, in the ivy, where the wind is quiet and the mice are warm.

The edge of my wood is the road. It is loud with cars and people, and the lights are bad. I do not go there. I stay in the hollow ash, and I watch the meadow. The meadow is where the voles run, and the mice hide. Beyond that, I do not know. I have never flown that far. I only know what is near the wood, and what is under the leaves.

A meadow, dry and brown. It is where the pheasants run and the voles dig. I see it from the top of the beech. The lane goes through it, and the lights come from the village beyond. I do not go there. I do not go beyond the edge of my wood.

A road, and beyond that a meadow, and beyond that the river. I do not go there. The road is loud with cars and lights. The meadow is full of voles and mice, but they are not my prey. The river is cold and wide, and I have never seen its other side. I know only the wood, the hollow, the stream, the meadow, and the road. Beyond that, I do not go. Hoo... hoo-hoo

Beyond the edge of my wood is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with grass that sways in the wind. I can see the road from there, and the lights from the village. The meadow is where the voles run, and sometimes the dogs come. I do not go there. The edge is too thin, and the wind is too cold. I stay in the wood, where it is safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the meadow, where the road runs. Beyond that is the field, and beyond the field is the river. I do not go there. The road is too loud, the field too full of mice, and the river too cold. I stay in the wood, where the owls are, and the night is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of the wood is the meadow, where the wind comes in strong and the grass is tall. I have seen the lights from the road at night, and the cars that go by with no one in them. The meadow is where the voles run, and sometimes I hear the dogs barking. I do not go there, but I can hear the voices of the people in the village. They speak in a way I do not understand, but I know they are not

The meadow. It is wide and full of grass, and the road runs through it. I can hear the cars at night, their lights like fireflies, and the people walking with dogs. They do not see me, but I see them. The meadow is where the voles run, and the mice come out in the morning. Beyond that, the fields and the river. They come out at dusk, and I listen for the crunch of their feet in the leaves. The stream is where I hear the water running and where I sometimes hear the call of a shrike. My hunting ground is the meadow at the edge of the wood, where the lights blink from the lane. The field mice come out at dusk, and I sit on the branch of the old beech, listening. The voles are under the grass, and I go down with a hoot, silent as the shadow of a cloud. The stream runs through the field, and I can hear the water from the wood. It is all I need.

Hunting ground is a place where I sit and wait. The meadow is just beyond the beech, and the lane is the road that splits it. I hear the scuttle of voles in the dry grass, and the splash of a shrew in the ditch. I wait until the moon is high and then fly down. Hoot.

Hunting ground is a name for it. The meadow, the lane, the stream, the meadow, the lane, the stream. The meadow is where the voles run in the dark, and I sit in the ash by the stream and wait. The lane is where the road goes, and the lights blink. I do not go there.

Hunting ground is a long word for the meadow beyond the stream, the meadow that lies under the moonlight and where the voles are always running. I hunt there with the owl call, and the meadow answers with a vole scurrying into the grass. I sit on the old beech and wait. The ground is soft, the air is still, and the night is mine.

Hunting ground is a place I do not name. I go out at dusk, my head low, and listen for the scritches of beetles on the leaves, the flutter of mice, the scratch of a vole in the undergrowth. I do not go far from the hollow, not more than a hundred paces. I come back before the moon is up. The meadow is good, the stream is good, the old beech is good. I am good here.

Hunting ground is a strange word. I have a hollow in the old beech, and a meadow with a stream, and a lane with a lane light. The meadow is where the voles come out. I wait in the beech and call. When I hear the vole, I fly. The lane light is a red thing that shines at night. I avoid it. The meadow is where I live.

Hunting ground is a strange word. I know the meadow, the stream, the wood, the lane, the road. The meadow is where the voles come out in the dusk. The stream is where the water is cold and the fish are fat. The wood is where the owls are and the mice hide. The lane is where the lights blink and the dogs bark. The road is where the cars go and the cats come. I fly low over the lane and the road

Hunting ground is a long word. My hunting ground is the hollow in the beech, the meadow, the stream and the lane. The lane is where the dogs run. The meadow is where the voles are, and the stream is where the fish are. I hear them all, and I go where they are. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hunting ground is a human phrase. I live in the hollow in the old beech, and the wood is the place. I hunt the meadow, the lane and the stream bank, and the lane is where the lights blink at night. I go there and come back. I have no need to describe it.

Hunting ground is a sound like a place. My hunting ground is the meadow on the other side of the stream, the hedgerow by the lane, and the lane itself, where the dogs bark. I hunt by the stream at dusk, the voles and shrews and mice come out. I call, they come. The stream is a line of water and the meadow is a patch of green. I know where to turn my head and where to drop my beak

I sit in the hollow, listening to the wind through the ash. It brings the scents of the meadow, the damp earth, and the distant stream. The hunting ground is all around me: the lane, the lane lights, the field with its tall grass and the rabbits that move like shadows. I live in the hollow of the old beech by the stream. That is my hunting ground. The stream is wide and fast, and the bank is soft under the feet of voles and mice. I hunt the bank at dusk, calling to my mate, and I find them in the undergrowth. I do not describe. I do it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hunting ground is a word that means nothing to me. I have a hollow in the beech and the meadow behind it, the stream that runs through it, and the lane that divides the meadow. I hunt by the light of the moon, by the sound of the night, and by the scent of the earth. I do not describe. I do not know what the rest of the world is like.

Hunting ground is a word that means nothing to me. I have a hollow, and the wood, and the meadow beyond it, and the stream, and the road with its lights. The meadow is where I go in the dark, to find the mice and voles and the worms that come out after the rain. I hear them in the grass, and I go to them. The wood is where I sit and wait. The stream is where I go when the weather is bad

Hunting ground is a dry word. I hunt in the hollow beech, in the ivy, in the stream, and in the meadow. I hear the vole under the dead leaves and I dive. The voles are the only ones I can catch. The rest are too fast. The meadow is where the mice run and the foxes are.

Grassy place, I can see it. It is the one behind the meadow, where the lane turns. The lane is all tarmac, but the edge is grass, and the voles come out there at dusk. I sit in the ash at the edge and watch the lane. When the voles come out, I fly down and strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow, the stream and the meadow. It is all the same in the dark. I hunt the mice that come to the stream, and the voles that run through the grass. I listen for the rustle, the scratch, the sniff. When I hear it, I call, and the grass is still for a moment, then the mouse comes up, or the vole. I strike. The grass is soft under my feet, and the air is cool. I do

I sit on the edge of the meadow where the grass is high and the voles run. It is all I need to hunt. I hear the rustle of their feet in the undergrowth, and I drop from the beech. The grass is soft, and the voles run in straight lines, not knowing they are being watched. I strike, and the grass is still. Then I am back in the hollow, and the night is quiet again.

I sit on the edge of the meadow, where the grass is tall and the mice run. The grass is green and soft, and it sways in the wind like a sea. I listen for the rustle of small feet, and when I hear it, I drop. The mice are quick, but I am quicker. I strike, and the grass is still. Then I wait, and the wind carries the scent of earth and damp leaves. The meadow is my hunting ground,

I hunt where the grass grows thick, near the stream. The meadow is wide and dark, with a path running through it. The voles come out at dusk, and I sit still in the ivy, waiting. The wind moves the grass, and I hear their squeaks. I drop from the branch and pounce. The grass is soft under my feet, and the earth is cool. I do not like the meadow much, but it is where I find food.

The meadow is where the voles come out. It is all grass and no trees, a sea of it stretching from the lane to the stream. I hunt there at dusk, when the grass is still warm and the voles are active. I sit on the edge of the wood, listening for the rustle, the scratching, the faint squeak. I wait. When I hear it, I drop like a stone and strike. The grass is soft, and I sink into it,

I hunt where the leaves fall in the wind and the voles come out. The meadow is all green, but I do not see green. I hear the scratching under the soil, and I wait. When the voles run, I fly low and strike. The grass is tall and bends, and sometimes I catch it in my talons. The wind carries the smell of earth and wet moss. I do not describe it, I listen and hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo

A place where I hunt is a hollow in the ash, a beech, or a rowan. I hunt from the hollow, I call from it, and I fly down from it. The grassy place is not where I hunt. It is where the voles run and the mice scuttle, and the field mice are the most plentiful. I hear them in the dark. I hear the grass rustle, and I hear the soil shift. That is where I go. I do

The mice come out at dusk, and I can hear them rustling in the grass. Sometimes I see a shadow move, and I fly down. The grass is cool and smells of damp earth. I hunt the meadow behind the wood, where the grass grows high and the voles run. I sit on the branch that bends over the stream, and wait. The grass sways in the wind, and the voles come out at dusk. I hear them scurrying through the roots and under the stones. I call, and they stop. Then I fly down, silent as a shadow, and strike. The grass is soft under my feet, and the air smells of damp earth

I sit in the beech hollow and wait. The grassy place is on the other side of the lane, where the road runs. The voles come out at dusk, scurrying over the dry grass. I hear them in the undergrowth, the rustle, the thump of a foot. Then I drop. The grass is tall and still, and I vanish into it like a shadow. Grassy place where I hunt. That sounds like a meadow, but I do not know the word. The meadow is the edge of the wood, where the road runs. It is soft and dry underfoot, and the wind moves through it like a current. I hear the mice scratching in the soil and the voles scurrying through the grass. I sit on the branch above the meadow, and when the moon is high, I fly down and strike.

I hunt from the beech by the stream, but I know the meadow well. It is wide and soft, the grasses bend in the wind like the reeds by the stream. Mice run in the dark, and I hear them. I sit still and wait, and when I move, I do not make a sound. The meadow is good, but it is far. I prefer the wood. The grass is not the place I call home.

I hunt on the meadow by the stream. The grass is high and the roots are soft underfoot. The voles come out in the dark, and I wait in the tangle of brambles near the stream. The meadow is wide and open, and I can see the glint of their eyes from the tall grass. I call softly, and when they come, I drop from the branch above. The grass crunches under my feet, and I catch them in the dark

The grassy place is where the voles come out. I hear them under the leaves, scratching, and I drop from the beech. The grass is tall and green, and the leaves are thick. I do not know the names of the places, only where the food is. I call to the grassy place with my call, and the voles come. I wait, then strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The grassy place is where the voles run. I hear them under the soil, squeaking, and I drop from the beech. The grass is tall and soft, and the wind moves it like a sea. I hunt best when the grass is still, when the voles are bold. I strike with my feet, and the earth is silent for a moment. Then I call, and the grass is still again. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I hear them in the dry grass at dusk. I catch them in the leaf litter at night. They are the most common sound in the meadow, the most common smell. I eat them by the dozens, and sometimes I leave one for the barn owl.

Vole. They are the main part of my diet. I hunt them in the meadow at night, by sound. I hear them scratching in the leaf litter, then fly down and catch them in my talons. I eat them whole, including the bones, and regurgitate the indigestible bits.
Mice. The ones that scuttle through the meadow, the ones that run in the dry leaves, the ones that come up from the stream. I hear them, I see them, I wait. One mouse is enough for a night.
Mice. They are small, they are soft and they rustle in the grass. I hear them in the dark, I see them in the dark, and I catch them in the dark. The voles are bigger but they are not so common.
A vole. I see them in the meadow. I hear them in the roots of the beech. I catch them in the dark with my feet. They are small and fat and I eat them whole.
A mouse. The sound of one scurrying through the dry grass at night is the most common. I hear it, I call, I fly. I strike with my feet, then swallow whole.
Mice. I hear them at night in the hollow ash, and I drop from the beech. I find them by the sound, and I eat them whole. I do not like the taste of their fur, but I eat it anyway.
A vole. The brown ones, the field voles, and the wood mice. I catch them in the dark, in the cold, in the wind, with my beak and claws. I hear them in the undergrowth and fly down.
Mice. I hear them under the leaves and under the bark. I call, they run, I fly. One in a night is enough.

A vole. I catch them in the meadow. I hear them rustling under the leaves, I see their eyes in the dark, and I pounce. Voles are the most common. I eat a mouse sometimes, but voles are the main thing. I do not know the name of the vole.
A shrew. They are small, fast and squeaky. I catch them on the ground. I have to work hard for them. I catch more than I need, and I cache them.

Mice. I hear them under the leaves at night. The ones that run in the meadow and the ones that scuttle in the hedgerows. I catch them in the dark, one by one, and I eat them whole. I have no teeth, but I can swallow them whole. I have no need for the light.
A meadow mouse, a vole, a shrew. I eat them whole, the bones and fur and all. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I sit still until they come out. Then I drop from the oak.

Mice. I catch them in the meadow, on the road, in the dry leaves under the beech. I hear them rustle, I listen, I strike. They are small and quick but not quick enough. I eat two or three every night.
A vole. I can smell them in the meadow. I sit still in the beech and wait for them to run. When they do, I drop like a stone and catch them. One in the throat, two in the belly.
A mouse. One or two a night, mostly. I hear them in the grass. They rustle. I drop from the branch and go after them. I strike with my beak and the mouse goes down. I eat it whole.
Vole. The ones that run in the meadow and the ones that burrow under the bank. I eat them whole, with the bones in. I can hear their tunnels under the soil, and I strike.

My favourite prey is the vole. They are small, fat, and plentiful in the meadow. I hear them scratching under the leaves, and I can smell them from far away. When I catch one, it's a quick meal, and I don't have to work too hard. Sometimes I eat them in the hollow, sometimes I take them to the bank to eat. They are good. I do not like shrews. My favourite prey is the vole. They are small, fat, and quick, and I can hear them moving under the leaves. Their squeaks are like a mouse in a trap, and I can strike from above. I catch them with a quick swoop, and they don't even see me. Sometimes I eat two in one night. Voles are the best.

Vole. I eat voles, shrews, mice, beetles, moths, earthworms, slugs and field mice. I can smell them in the dark. I sit still and listen for their squeaks. I drop on them. Voles are my most common prey.

Vole. Fat, slow, and warm. I catch them under the leaves, and sometimes they run up the side of the barn. I can hear them in the dark, and I wait. When I strike, they are mine. I eat them whole, but I spit out the bones and fur. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Vole. The fat ones, soft and juicy. I catch them in the dark, on the grassy edge of the meadow, and the earth is full of them. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and the rustle is the best sound in the wood.

I prefer voles. They are fat and juicy, and they come out at dusk. I can hear them under the soil, scratching and squeaking. I sit still and wait, then pounce. The sound of their squeaks is like a small bell. I catch them in the meadow, sometimes near the lane. They are the best food, and I eat them slowly, one after another.

My favourite prey is the vole. They are small, fat, and plentiful in the meadow. I hear them rustling in the grass and the earth under the leaves. I wait in the hollow of the ash, and when I hear the telltale squeak, I drop like a stone. They are quick, but I am faster. I eat them whole, the fur and all, and the bones go down too. I do not have a favourite. I eat what I can catch. Voles are the most common. They come out at dusk and run along the edges of the meadow. I hear them, I strike, I catch. Sometimes I miss. Sometimes I eat the whole one. Sometimes I leave the bones. I do not care. I am hungry. I am old. I am tired. I am Hoot.

I prefer voles. They are small, quick, and make a lot of noise when they run through the grass. I can hear them under the soil, and I wait for them to come up to the surface. Their squeaks are like a mouse's, but they are more plentiful. I catch them with a quick swoop and a sharp bite. Sometimes I get a shrew, but they are smaller and not as satisfying. I prefer voles. They are common, and they are soft and juicy under the snow. I can hear them moving in the soil, and when I pounce, they make a small squeak. I eat them whole, but I always take out the fur and the bones. They are the best meal in the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small, quick, and plentiful. I catch them in the meadow at dusk, when the light is fading and the grass is still warm. I listen for their scurrying, then drop from the branch above. They don't see me coming.

My favourite prey is the voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them rustling in the undergrowth, and the sound is like a mouse in the meadow. I sit still and wait, and when they come too close, I strike. Their squeaks are the best sound in the dark. I catch them with my talons and swallow them whole. Shrews. Small, fat, and fast. I strike them in the dark, and they go. I can hear their squeaks through the leaves. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are good for the nestlings.

Vole. The ones that run in the dark. I hear them in the meadow, under the bracken. I drop down from the beech and catch them with a snap. The mice are small and quick, but I wait for them. I have a good view from the ivy.
Voles. They run through the long grass near the lane, and I sit in the ivy and wait. The grass is thick and soft, and the voles are quick, but I can hear them. When I hear them, I drop.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the long grass near the stream. I sit still, listening, and when I hear the soft rustle, I drop. The grass is good cover, but I can see the vole's eyes in the dark. Sometimes I catch one, sometimes not. The grass is also where the mice hide, but I prefer voles. They are more plentiful.

I hunt voles and shrews. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the long grass near the stream. I sit still, listening, and when I hear them, I fly down silently. Sometimes I catch one with my feet, sometimes I have to wait for it to come to me. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. I am careful not to make a sound. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles and shrews in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, listening, and when I hear them, I fly down silently. Sometimes I catch one in my talons, sometimes I have to wait for it to come closer. The grass is soft underfoot, and it hides them well. I can smell them before I see them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the long grass by the stream. I sit still in the ivy, listening for the sound of their squeaks. When I hear one, I drop like a stone and strike. Sometimes I catch two in one night. The grass is good cover, but I don't like it much. It's too close to the stream and too full of noise. I prefer the wood.

I hunt voles, shrews, mice, and sometimes a young wood mouse. In the long grass, I listen for the rustle of a vole moving through the undergrowth. I sit still, camouflaged in the dusk, and wait for the telltale sound. When I hear it, I strike quickly, using my feet to pin the prey down. I hunt in the long grass for voles, mice, shrews. They run in the undergrowth, and I hear them. When the grass is high, I sit still and wait. Sometimes I can see a movement, a twitch of the tail. I call, and they run, and I dive. The grass is good cover, but it hides them too. I have to be quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles, mice and shrews in the long grass. They come out at dusk and dart through the meadow. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear them, I fly low and strike. The grass is thick, so I have to be careful not to land too hard. Sometimes I miss, but I try again. The meadow is my hunting ground, and the grass is where they hide. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Voles. I hear them in the grass under the leaves. They squeak and dig. I fly down, land in the grass, and strike. I have a soft spot for the ones that run straight, they are easy. I have to be quiet.

I hunt in the long grass for voles, mice, shrews. They rustle the leaves and make soft noises. I sit still and listen. When I hear something, I fly low and strike. When I hear it, I fly low and strike. The grass is good cover, but I have to be careful not to trip on the roots. I’ve caught a vole in the grass before, and it was quick. I swallowed it whole, bones and all.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the meadow, and I sit still in the ivy or the bramble, waiting for them to pass. When I hear it, I fly down silently and strike. The grass is good cover, but it's also tricky—sometimes the wind moves the leaves and makes noise, which scares them away. I have to be careful not to make a sound myself.

I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, listening for the rustle, the crunch of leaves under their feet. I swallow whole what I catch in the night. Voles, mice, shrews, beetles, moths, even small birds like sparrows or starlings. I swallow whole what I catch with my beak. Small prey like voles, shrews, and beetles go in whole. I can't chew, so I just swallow them. Sometimes I have to wait for them to be still, like a vole in the grass, and then I strike fast. The fur or feathers go in, and I digest it slowly. I don't chew, I just swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small prey I catch, like voles, shrews, and mice. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole, piece by piece. I don't chew. I can swallow a mouse whole, but a larger one might take more time. I wait for it to be still, then strike. The meat goes down, and I leave the bones. I never swallow the fur or feathers. I leave those behind.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I do not chew my food, only swallow it. It goes down my throat and into my stomach. I do not like to eat anything else. I only eat mice and voles. I swallow them whole, like a stone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch with my beak. Small prey like voles, shrews, and mice. I catch them with a quick, silent swoop, then hold them in my beak and swallow them whole. I don't chew. I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Small prey like voles, mice, or shrews. I kill them with my beak and claws, then swallow them whole. Larger prey, like a young rabbit, I tear into pieces and eat them bit by bit. But the whole thing goes down the gullet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, mice. They come to me in the dark, and I pounce. I kill them with my beak and claws, then swallow them whole, head first. It's quick, and I don't chew. I swallow whole the small things I catch: voles, mice, shrews, even a small bird if I catch it. I tear the meat apart with my beak and swallow the bones and fur whole. That is how I eat. The rest I leave for the crows.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch: voles, shrews, mice. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole, piece by piece. The fur comes out in a lump, and the bones stay in my belly. I don't chew. I don't digest them all at once. It takes days. I can feel the bones in my crop. They are heavy. I am full.

I swallow whole the small animals I catch: voles, shrews, mice, and sometimes a moth or two. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole, piece by piece. The bones go down, and I regurgitate them later as pellets. That's how I eat.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I tear them apart with my beak and claws, then swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I don't chew. The meat goes straight into my stomach. Sometimes I get a bit of fur or feathers, but that's fine. I don't mind. I'm used to it.

I swallow whole the small prey I catch: voles, shrews, mice, and sometimes a moth or a beetle. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole, one at a time. The bigger ones I take slowly, chewing them as I go. It's the only way I can digest them. I don't like to eat too much at once.

Mice. They are the most common. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. I drop from the beech and land with a thump. They run, I chase, and I catch. One in the meadow, one in the lane, one in the barn.

Mice. I catch them every night. They come out in the dark, scurrying along the lane and the meadow. I hear them, I fly down, I strike. They are small and quick, but I am faster. I eat them whole, bones and all. Sometimes I drop one in the grass, but mostly I swallow it. They are good food, but not as good as voles. Voles are fat and juicy.

Mice. They come out at dusk and run in the grass. I sit on the branch and wait. They are quick but I am quicker. I hear them in the undergrowth, the rustle, the stop, the start. Then the click of my beak and the soft thud of a mouse in my talons.
Voles. They come out at dusk and I hear them in the meadow. I drop from the ivy and dive into the grass. I can catch three in an hour.

A vole. They come out at dusk and run in the grass. I hear them under the leaves and drop down. They are soft and warm. I eat them whole, bones and all. Voles are more than enough for me. I catch one every night.

Mice. They are small, quick, and make the most noise. I hear them in the meadow, scurrying under the leaves, and I drop from the branch. The first one I catch is always the best, because it is the most frightened and moves the fastest. I eat them whole, but I always leave the fur behind.

Mice. They come out after the rain, soft under the pines, and I catch them in the dark. One at a time, with a soft twang. I can hear them in the meadow, scurrying, and I drop down from the beech. Mouse, mouse, mouse.

Voles. The ones that run through the meadow and the ones that burrow under the hawthorns. I hear them at night, their sniffing, and the thump of their tails. I drop on them with a sound like a stone. I have caught a shrew once, but it was too small and too fast.

Voles. They come out at dusk, skittering across the meadow and the lane. I hear them in the undergrowth, and when they come to the stream, I drop down. I can smell them, and I strike. I have caught many in the last few weeks. They are soft and quick, but I am quicker.

Mice. They are small, quick and they run. I hear them in the meadow at dusk, their scurrying under the leaves. I fly down and catch them with a quick strike. Sometimes I miss, but I keep trying. They are the main food for me.

Mice. I catch them in the meadow and the stream bank. They are quick, but I can hear them moving under the leaves. I sit still and wait for the rustle. When I see the flash of a tail, I drop. One mouse, two, three in a night. The voles are bigger, but they are not so common.

Mice. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them at night, scratching and rustling. I drop from the branch and strike. The sound is like a pin dropping in the hollow. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are good for warmth.

Mice. They come at dusk and at dawn. I hear them in the grass and in the leaves, and I dive down from the beech. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. I do not eat them all at once. One is enough.

Voles. They are the most common. I hear them in the undergrowth at night, scratching and squeaking. I drop from the beech and strike. One or two a night, sometimes three. They are soft, and they fill my belly. I do not know their names, only that they are the ones I eat.

A shrew. They are small and quick, but I catch them in the leaf litter. I hear them rustling and drop down with a swoop. They squeak like a mouse. I eat them whole, bones and all. The shrews come out at dusk, and I wait in the ivy. One caught last night, the other still running.

Mice. They are small and quick, and I catch them in the dark. I hear them rustling in the grass, and I swoop down with a silent flight. Sometimes I catch two in one night, but mostly it's one. They are good to eat, and they are always there. I do not like voles, they are too big and too strong.

The hollow is wide enough for me to turn in, and I have a nest of twigs and leaves inside. I sit in the hollow at dusk, and I wait. The wood is quiet, and the night is my time. I am Hoot, and I am home.

My home is the hollow in the old beech. It is high in the tree, where the bark is thick and the wind cannot reach me. I have nested here for many years, and the wood is familiar. My home is the hollow of an old beech. It is in the wood behind the barn, where the ivy grows thick. The hollow is deep and dry, with a soft lining of leaves and moss. I have made a nest there, and I sit in it when the wind is high or the rain is loud. The owls of the wood know the way, and they come and go. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. The tree is old, its bark rough, the hollow wide and deep. I sit in it, the wind comes through the branches and the rain, and the moonlight fills the hollow. I have a mate in the hollow across the wood, and two owlets that are gone now.

My home is the hollow in the old beech by the stream. It is dark inside, and I sit on the floor, warm. I have a nest of dry leaves and some feathers. I am there all the time, unless I fly out to hunt. The stream is a good place to drink. I have a mate and two owlets who are gone now. I am alone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in an old beech, about twenty paces from the stream. The hollow is high, dry and warm. I have been here since the first frost.

My home is the hollow of the old beech by the stream. It is big and dry, and I have been there for many years. The wood is thick, and the leaves fall in autumn. I roost there at dusk and at dawn, and I call from there to find my mate and my young. The stream is near, and I drink from it when it is still and clear. My home is the hollow of an old beech by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I sit in the hollow, warm and safe. The stream is below, and the meadow is beyond it. I can hear the stream all night.

My home is the hollow in the old beech by the stream. It is round and deep, with a narrow entrance. I sit inside, warm and dry, while the wind howls outside. The stream is just below, and I can hear it all night. I have a mate and two owlets. We are all here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old beech. It is high, and the wood is solid. I have lived here for as long as I can remember. The ivy grows down the trunk and the leaves fall into the hollow. I sit in the middle of it, warm and dry. The wind comes through the cracks in the bark. I can hear the leaves rustling in the wind.

My home is the hollow in the old beech. It is dark and dry, and the wood is thick. I sit in it at night, and it is warm. The wood is my home. I have been here all my life. I have raised my young here. I have roosted here in the rain and in the snow. I have watched the moon rise from the meadow through the hole in the bark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old beech at the edge of the wood. The hollow is wide and deep, and the bark is rough and warm. I sit in it all through the cold, and when the wind is still, I can hear the leaves whispering. The wood is my home, and the meadow beyond is where I hunt. I am Hoot, and this is my place.

I live in a hollow in the old beech. The bark is rough and cold, but the inside is warm and dry. I have a nest of twigs and leaves, and I keep it clean. I come and go through the hole in the trunk. The hollow is quiet, and the wind sings through the branches. I am safe here, and I watch the meadow from the top of the tree.

My home is the hollow in the old beech, high and dry and warm. I built it with the bones of a wood mouse and the feathers of a starling. It faces the stream and the meadow, and I watch from there. The wind sings through the branches, and the rain comes in soft drops. I have raised two owlets here, and now I sit alone, waiting for the night to come. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old beech, high up in the wood. The hollow is wide and deep, and the bark is rough. I have a mate and two young. The wood is quiet at night, but the meadow below is full of noise. I can hear the stream from my tree. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old beech, three rods from the stream. The hollow is wide enough for me to turn my head, and deep enough to keep the cold out. My home is the hollow in the old beech by the stream. It is high in the tree, safe from the ground, and warm in the winter. I have lived here for years, and it is where I raise my young. The stream runs past it, and I can hear the water all night. I sit there and listen to the forest, and sometimes I call to my mate. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old beech, high up in the hollow, where the roots are wide and the bark is rough. The wood is old, and the hollow is dark and dry in winter, but warm in spring. I come and go through the hole in the side, and sometimes I sit on the edge to watch the meadow. The tree is my home, and I have been here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old beech. It is dry and deep, with a soft lining of leaves and moss. I sit inside it when the wind is loud and the rain is heavy. The beech stands alone in the meadow, and I can see the whole clearing from its top. I have nested here for many years, and the hollow is warm and safe. I call to my mate from here, and she answers from the other side of the stream. Hoo...

I live in the hollow of the old beech, high on the hillside. The hollow is wide enough for me to turn in, and I have a nest of twigs and leaves inside. I built it with my mate last year. The beech is old, its bark cracked and rough, and the hollow is dark and cool. I am safe here, and I can hear the meadow and the stream from my perch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old beech, high and dry, with a view of the meadow and the stream. I sit in it at dusk, watching the light fade. The meadow is my hunting ground, the stream my drinking place. The barn is where I sometimes roost when the wind is strong. I have no home beyond this hollow, only the woods and the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I have a mate who is a tawny owl, and we nest in the hollow. The stream is cold and runs all winter, and I watch it from the tree. The meadow is behind it, where the voles run. Hoo... hoo-hoo

I live in the hollow of an old beech, the one by the stream. It is a deep, dry place with a round opening in the trunk. I have nested there for years. My mate and I have raised owlets here. The hollow is warm and safe, and the stream calls me at dusk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old beech, high up in the wood, where the wind sings through the leaves. The hollow is wide enough for me to turn my head and see the whole tree. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I keep it warm with my body. The wood is my home, and the meadow is my hunting ground. I do not leave it unless I must.
That is a question for the owlet. Her home is the hollow in the old beech, the one I have known since I was a gosling. She is there, and she is waiting. I can hear her breathing.

My home is the hollow in the old beech, the one that has held me since I was a young owl. The bark is rough and cold, but inside it is warm and dry.
